issues.issue: The offering is described as made to "qualified institutional purchasers," which cannot be squared with the cover legend furnishing the Memorandum to "qualified institutional or accredited investors" or with the Declaration of Trust's Recital (b) and the Subscription Agreement's representation that each subscriber is a "qualified purchaser." Who is eligible to buy Shares therefore turns on which of these three formulations governs.

The Declaration is incorporated "as further amended from time to time," so it is unclear whether the terms described in this Memorandum are those in force on October 24, 2000 or whatever the Trustee later substitutes under the amendment power described in the "Amendment of Declaration of Trust" provision. The provision fixes no date at which the governing text is ascertained.

This purpose statement — a "continuous source of managed investment for cash collateral" — is of the kind argued to control the operative investment terms, and it sits against the Portfolio Diversification list and the five-year maximum maturity provision, which permit long-dated and illiquid holdings. Whether the stated purpose limits those guidelines is open.

"Currently serves as the sole trustee" leaves the trusteeship contingent, while Declaration §§2.2–2.3 permit the Trustee to add or appoint successor trustees without Shareholder action. The Memorandum nowhere states what becomes of the described arrangements if the trustee changes.

Shareholder status is conditioned on "payment of the consideration specified by Wells Fargo from time to time," which fixes no price mechanism, whereas Declaration §4.5 credits investments at the Net Asset Value next determined and Subscription Agreement §4 measures the contribution by the collateral received on securities loans. Which measure sets the subscription price is unresolved.

Wells Fargo's appointment of itself as investment manager stands against Declaration §6.1, which contemplates management contracts and forbids retaining the Trustee or its affiliates to provide additional services for additional compensation beyond that disclosed in the securities lending agreements. Whether a self-appointment is such a contract, and on what terms, is not addressed.

Galliard is retained "to advise" Wells Fargo on "managing a portion of the Fund," leaving unclear whether Galliard has discretionary authority over that portion or only an advisory role, and which entity is answerable for its selections. "Advise" is not defined anywhere in the Memorandum.

The "Specific portion" advised by Galliard may vary "in the sole discretion of Wells Fargo," with no floor, ceiling, or notice requirement, so the extent of Galliard's role is indeterminate. Nothing in the Memorandum measures the discretion.

Shares are stated flatly to be uncertificated, while Declaration §4.7(b) makes Shares uncertificated "unless expressly authorized by the Trustee" and allows the Trustee to authorize certificates. The two cannot both be read as fixing the form of Shares.

"Undivided proportionate interest in all assets and liabilities of the Fund ... without priority or preference over any other Share" conflicts with Declaration §4.1, which makes each Share equal "except to the extent affected by expense allocations," and with §4.2, which lets the Trustee create Shares of a Series with differing preferences and rights. Whether Shares can in fact be non-uniform is thus in doubt.

The undertaking to "seek to maintain a relatively stable value per Share" cannot be squared with the Valuation provision requiring the Fund's assets to be valued each Business Day at "then current market value," which by definition moves the per-Share value. "Relatively stable" is also given no benchmark.

Shares are offered at "the then applicable value per Share (as defined below)," but no definition of "value per Share" appears below — the Valuation section speaks only of valuing assets at current market value, and the redemption provision speaks of "the valuation per Share as determined by Wells Fargo." The cross-reference points to nothing.

The sentence never states a minimum required investment, leaving the amount wholly to Wells Fargo's determination "in the efficient management of the securities lending program," a standard with no content. As written the clause is incomplete and unenforceable as a term.

Daily valuation at "then current market value" cannot be squared with the Terms of the Offering and Investment Objectives provisions promising a relatively stable/$10.00 per-Share value, nor with Declaration §5.3, which requires Net Asset Value to be determined "in a manner consistent with the 1940 Act" (permitting amortized cost). Which valuation method governs the Share price is the central unresolved point.

"Certain other recordkeeping and accounting services" is unbounded, and the same section then assigns "certain of the accounting services" to Forum Accounting Services. Which services each performs cannot be told from the text.

The mandatory daily dividend declaration conflicts with Declaration §5.1, which provides that the Trustee "may declare and pay dividends" and fixes their amount, form and timing in its discretion. The garbled subject ("The ives") also leaves it unstated who is obliged to declare.

The Fund is said to bear expenses of acquisition, ownership and transfer of investments, audit expenses and indemnification expenses, whereas Declaration Article Seven charges the Trust or Series with a far longer list including advisers' and Trustee's fees, legal and compliance expenses and litigation costs. Whether the Memorandum's narrower enumeration limits what may be charged to the Fund is open.

The flat statement that neither Wells Fargo nor its affiliates will receive any fees or compensation from the Trust conflicts with Declaration §2.6 (Trustee may receive compensation as it fixes) and §3.1(k) (power to pay itself reasonable compensation from Trust Property). The Trustee's 40% share of net securities-lending earnings under the securities lending agreement sharpens the question.

The Forum accounting contract is "entered into by Wells Fargo," yet the provision does not say whether the Trust or Wells Fargo pays for it, and the Expenses provision listing what the Fund bears does not include accounting fees. Who bears this cost is left unresolved.

The fee is payable to "Forum Financial," an entity nowhere identified, while the preceding sentence contracts with "Forum Accounting Services, LLC." The mismatch leaves the payee, and whether they are the same person, uncertain.

Use of affiliated brokers "subject to any applicable law" sits against the final paragraph of Declaration §3.1, which requires the Trustee to comply with the affiliated-transaction prohibitions of 1940 Act §17(a), (d) and (e) as if the Trust were registered. Whether that Declaration constraint qualifies this permission is not addressed.

"Shares of the Fund may not be transferred or assigned" conflicts with the Subscription Agreement §5.h, which states that transfers of Shares may be made with the consent of the Trustee in its sole discretion, and with the Declaration's definition of Shares as "transferable units of interest." Whether the bar is absolute or consent-based is unresolved.

Redemption "at a redemption price equal to the valuation per Share as determined by Wells Fargo" conflicts with Declaration §5.2, which sets the price at Net Asset Value next determined after receipt of the redemption request. The two give different prices and different pricing times.

The promise that payment for redeemed Shares "will be made in cash within seven days" conflicts with Declaration §5.2, which allows payment of the redemption price wholly or partly in securities and caps suspension at seven days. Whether a Shareholder can be paid in kind turns on which text controls.

This exculpation preserves liability for ordinary "negligence," while Declaration §8.1 excepts only "bad faith, gross negligence, willful misconduct or reckless disregard." The standard of care owed by Wells Fargo therefore differs depending on which instrument governs.

Indemnity is denied here where the loss was caused by the person's own "negligence," whereas Declaration §8.2 mandates indemnification of Covered Persons "to the fullest extent permitted under the Maryland Act" subject only to §8.1's gross-negligence carve-out. The two indemnity regimes cannot both be given effect.

Shareholders are given "the same limitation of liability extended to stockholders of a business corporation," while Declaration §4.10 measures it by stockholders of "a private corporation for profit organized under the General Corporation Law of the State of Maryland." The reference class of the limitation differs between the two.

Shareholder indemnity is promised "from the assets of the Trust," whereas Declaration §8.3 limits it to "the assets belonging to the applicable Series" and §4.6(b) makes Series assets answerable only for that Series' obligations. Which pool of assets backs the indemnity is in conflict.

The trailing qualifier "unless expressly required under the Maryland Act" is misplaced and it cannot be told whether it qualifies the Trustee's power to amend, the absence of Shareholder approval, or the notice deemed given to purchasers. Declaration §9.7's proviso that Shareholders may vote on amendments the Trustee submits is also omitted here.

"The obligations of Wells Fargo to the Trust are not exclusive" sits against Declaration §3.3, which makes the Trustee an ERISA fiduciary held to the prudent-person standard for plan-asset Shareholders, and against the liability provision preserving liability for negligence. How far non-exclusivity qualifies those duties is unstated.

The assurance that investment decisions are made "independently from those other accounts" is difficult to square with Declaration §3.2, which expressly permits the Trustee to buy from, sell to, or lend Trust assets to affiliated persons, and with the affiliated-broker provision of this Memorandum. What independence means in that setting is left open.

The sentence is broken mid-clause ("the Trust and Wells Fa continue in that capacity"), so it cannot be told whether KPMG audits the Trust alone or Wells Fargo as well, or who may terminate the engagement. The retention is in any event subject only to Wells Fargo's "sole discretion," with no independence protection.

The text is scrambled and the commencement date is stated twice in incompatible fragments ("July 2" / "y 2, 2001"), leaving the operative date of the Fund uncertain. Nothing else in the Memorandum fixes it.

The objective of a positive return over the daily Fed Funds rate with "safety of principal and daily liquidity" as the prime considerations cannot easily be squared with the guidelines allowing 15% illiquid securities and a five-year maximum maturity. Whether the stated objective constrains those specific permissions is open.

The sentence is incomplete and unreadable ("securities wi har ide a y : th fixed, variable, or floating"), so the permitted rate structures cannot be determined from its own words. Any reading has to be supplied from the variable-rate limits elsewhere in the Investment Policies.

The Fund "will endeavor to maintain a stable $10.00 price per Share" while the same sentence disclaims any assurance of it, so the provision states both an undertaking and its negation without saying what effort is owed. "Endeavor" is given no content.

The first sentence requires obligations rated in the highest short-term category "by one of two nationally recognized statistical reporting organizations," while the next sentence requires the highest rating from "at least one" NRSRO — one or two ratings cannot both be the test. The provision also permits unrated obligations "determined to be of comparable quality by Wells Fargo" with no stated criteria.

The Investment Manager is "authorized to invest assets of the Fund in" a closed list of nine categories with no catch-all, and the categories themselves ("asset-backed securities," "corporate notes, bonds, debentures," "commercial paper and participations") are undefined. Whether structured or hybrid instruments fall inside those categories, or are excluded because unlisted, is the question the list raises.

The 5% cap is by "obligations of any one issuer" measured only "at the time of purchase," but the provision does not say who the issuer is for asset-backed, pass-through or repurchase-agreement exposures, nor whether the limit must be restored after it is breached by later events. The term "issuer" carries more than one reasonable meaning for the instruments the list authorizes.

The 35% cap applies to "variable rate securities," but the Investment Objectives provision distinguishes "fixed, variable, or floating" rate securities, leaving it open whether floating rate instruments count against the cap. The distinction is nowhere defined.

"Illiquid securities as that term is defined in the SEC's Rule 2a-7" imports a definition from a rule applicable to registered money market funds that the Fund does not follow, and Rule 2a-7's own illiquidity limit differs from the 15% stated here. What the incorporated definition covers is uncertain.

The logic is inverted: private placements are "generally considered liquid unless at least two broker/dealers provide an active secondary market," so on its face the existence of active market makers makes a security illiquid. The mechanical error reverses the intended test.

The 20% overnight floor states no measuring date — unlike the 5% and 35% limits, which are expressly tested "at the time of purchase" — so whether it is a continuous requirement or a purchase-time test is unresolved. Nor is "assets scheduled to mature overnight" defined for repurchase agreements or demand instruments.

The 90-day dollar-weighted average maturity is imposed on "the Trust's portfolio," while the surrounding guidelines limit "the Fund," and the Declaration establishes multiple separate Series each with its own guidelines. Whether the maturity test is applied to the Enhanced Yield Fund or across the whole Trust is not settled by the words used.

The rule directs use of "the shortest of the following" but the ensuing sentence deems a variable rate demand obligation's maturity to be "the longer of" the reset period or the demand recovery period, so the two commands contradict each other within the provision. The enumeration also labels two different clauses "(ii)."

A five-year maximum maturity cannot readily be squared with the Portfolio Quality provision, which permits only obligations carrying the highest short-term rating category from an NRSRO — a rating class that does not attach to five-year paper. Which of the two limits the eligible universe is unresolved.

This subsection uses "the shorter of" the next interest rate adjustment or the demand recovery period for variable and floating rate obligations, while the Portfolio Maturity subsection deems a variable rate demand obligation's maturity to be "the longer of" those same two periods. The same instrument gets two different maturities under the two provisions.

Using "the end date of the agreement" gives no answer for open or continuing repurchase agreements, which have no fixed end date, and the sentence is missing the punctuation that would separate the condition from the rule. The maturity of such repos is therefore indeterminate.

The operative consequence of a downgrade is missing from the sentence — it breaks off at "the Investment [Manager] ... determines is in the best Interests of the Trust," so no verb states what the Investment Manager must do (sell, hold, or report). As written there is no ascertainable obligation on a downgrade.

"Requisite NRSROs" and "Unrated Security" are used as defined terms but are defined nowhere, and the Portfolio Quality provision requires the highest rating from only one NRSRO. The plural "Requisite NRSROs" cannot be reconciled with that single-rating standard.

Investment in "an unregistered investment company conforming to the requirements of Rule 2a-7" gives no test of conformity and no one to make the determination, and the parenthetical is introduced by "i.e.," leaving it unclear whether the two examples exhaust what is permitted. Investment companies also appear nowhere in the authorized-investment list.

"A leading money market index such as Fed Funds or LIBOR" gives two specifics after an open-ended general phrase, so which other indices qualify as "leading" is unresolved. The word "leading" is given no measure.

"Dual index and inverse floaters" are prohibited without definition, and naming only those two structures raises the expressio unius question whether other structured floaters are permitted. The scope of the prohibition depends on that reading.

This risk factor assumes the Trust may have "the counterparty to a derivative," yet derivatives appear nowhere in the Portfolio Diversification list of authorized investments. Whether derivative exposure is permitted turns on reconciling the two.

The acknowledgment that the Trust may be unable to sell illiquid securities at an advantageous time or price sits against the Investment Objectives provision, which makes "daily liquidity requirements" a prime consideration, and the 15% illiquid allowance. How much illiquidity the Fund may carry is left to be read out of the whole instrument.

The state-law limb is self-cancelling — sales will be made "where available, upon either appropriate exemptions from state registration or qualification requirements, or pursuant to such registration or qualification" — so it commits to nothing ascertainable. Reliance on Rule 506 also sits against the cover legend offering to "institutional or accredited" investors without stating the number permitted.

The provision invokes the "1946 Act," which does not exist; the intended reference is the Investment Company Act of 1940 defined in the heading and used in the next sentence. The mechanical error leaves the statute relied on unnamed in this sentence.

Reliance on the Section 3(c)(1) exemption (not more than 100 beneficial owners) conflicts with Recital (b) of the Declaration of Trust, which states the Trustee's intention that the Trust be exempt under the Section 3(c)(7) qualified purchaser exemption, and with the Subscription Agreement's "qualified purchaser" representation. The two exemptions impose different eligibility conditions on Shareholders.

"Appropriate representations and undertakings" to assure that the "conditions of beneficial ownership" are met on an ongoing basis names neither the representations nor the condition, and Declaration §4.4 supplies a different counting rule (100 Shareholders, with look-through for flow-through entities). What Wells Fargo must actually obtain is not ascertainable.

The provision breaks off at "the rules and regulations of the United States Department of," so the ERISA discussion is incomplete and says nothing about whether Trust assets are plan assets. Declaration §3.3 and §8.5 by contrast make the Trustee an ERISA fiduciary held to the prudent-person standard for plan Shareholders.

"The Trust and the Fund are classified as partnerships for Federal income tax purposes" contradicts Section 9.1 of the October 24, 2000 Declaration of Trust, which provides that "This Declaration creates a trust and not a partnership" — a conflict cured only by the November 2001 First Amendment. Which characterization governed when Shares were sold is open.

Wells Fargo's stated intent to "restrict transfers of ownership" presupposes transfers that may be permitted, whereas the Transferability provision states flatly that Shares "may not be transferred or assigned" and Declaration §4.9 voids any purported transfer. The two describe different transfer regimes.

Allocations of income, gain, loss and deduction are said to be "determined according to the Declaration of Trust," but the October 24, 2000 Declaration contains no allocation provisions — capital accounts and the §704 allocation methodology were only added by the November 2001 First Amendment to Section 9.1. The cross-reference points to terms that did not then exist.
"Will be passed on by KPMG LLP" does not say whether a tax opinion has been or will be delivered, to whom, or whether investors may rely on it. "Passed on" carries more than one meaning here.

"Should be exempt" and "should not cause a Shareholder to be subject to tax" state predictions rather than terms, and no standard is given for the assumed absence of "any other nexus to Maryland." Whether any assurance is given at all is the question.

Describing the Memorandum as merely "an overview" sits against the cover legend qualifying it in its entirety by the Declaration of Trust, and against Subscription Agreement §5.b, by which the Subscriber relies solely on the facts and terms set forth in the Confidential Memorandum and the other furnished documents. Whether the Memorandum's descriptions are binding terms or non-operative summary is thus in issue.

"Any other materials available to Wells Fargo relating to the Trust" is unbounded and it is not said which materials must be produced on request, while the cover legend limits authorized information to this Memorandum and "the supplemental data to be furnished or made available." The scope of the invitation cannot be fixed from the words.

The blanket bar on "divulgence of any of its contents without the prior written consent of Wells Fargo" cannot be squared with the ERISA provision directing fiduciaries to "review with their legal advisors" whether holding Shares is permissible, or with the tax provision directing investors to consult their own tax advisers. Whether disclosure to a recipient's advisers is prohibited is left unresolved.

The return obligation is triggered "promptly upon delivery of updated offering materials, upon reaching a decision not to subscribe, or if such subscription is not accepted," but nothing states what a recipient who does subscribe may retain, and "reaching a decision" is a purely internal event with no verifiable moment. The trigger is unascertainable in operation.
